article_title: TimescaleDB 2.32.1 Fixes a Scheduler Bug That Failed Every Background Job, a Week After 2.32.0 Enabled Adaptive Integer Compression

content_preview.title: TimescaleDB 2.32.1 Fixes a Scheduler Bug That Failed Every Background Job, a Week After 2.32.0 Enabled Adaptive Integer Compression
content_preview.summary: TimescaleDB 2.32.1, released November 19, 2026, fixes a scheduler bug that failed every background job on PostgreSQL's newest minor releases, about a week after 2.32.0 made Adaptive Integer Compression the default.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

TimescaleDB 2.32.1, released November 19, 2026, fixes a bug that, according to the project's own release notes on [GitHub](https://github.com/timescale/timescaledb/releases/tag/2.32.1), meant "every job run by the scheduler fails" on PostgreSQL's newest minor releases. The patch lands about a week after TimescaleDB 2.32.0 turned on Adaptive Integer Compression (AIC) by default, according to [GitHub](https://github.com/timescale/timescaledb/releases/tag/2.32.0) and the project's [cha...

editor_notes.content_quality: Clean News-category write-up (553 words, within the 400-1200 range) structured as Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know. Claims are consistently hedged with attribution ('according to GitHub', 'per its release notes') and direct quotes are set off in quotation marks rather than paraphrased as fact.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 4 sources fetched successfully (HTTP 200, no suspicious_patterns, sha256 of decompressed snapshots matches manifest). Read all 4 raw snapshots directly (source-0.html.gz = GitHub release page 2.32.0, source-1.html.gz = GitHub release page 2.32.1, source-2.html.gz = raw CHANGELOG.md, source-3.html.gz = PostgreSQL.org announcement). Verified verbatim: 'every job run by the scheduler fails' (source-1 and source-2), 'Enable Adaptive Integer Compression (AIC) by default' and 'a larger set of security fixes than usual' (source-0), 'chooses the best encoding for each block of integer values' / 'results in the up to 20% improvement in compression ratios for integers, while queries benefiting from faster decompression perform up to two times better' / 'will be enabled by default in the `2.32.0` release' (source-2, 2.31.0 entry), 'fully backward compatible with older Postgres minor versions' and the 'strongly recommend' upgrade-order language (source-2). Confirmed the PG version caps (18.6/17.11/16.15 in 2.32.0, 18.7/17.12/16.16 in 2.32.1) and the continuous-aggregate watermark, background-worker-start/stop/restart-by-owner, telemetry-job-owner, READ COMMITTED skip-rows, and 992-row-crash bugfix items all appear verbatim in source-0. Confirmed PR #11015 ('Fix background jobs failing on new PostgreSQL minor releases') and the erikdarlingdata 'Thanks' credit in source-2's 2.32.1 entry. Confirmed the PostgreSQL.org page (source-3) is dated 2026-11-12 and covers 18.7/17.12/16.16/15.20/14.25 and 19 RC 2, matching the article's description. The internal link to the prior PostgreSQL article (/article/2026-11/13-postgresql-november-updates-...) resolves to an existing file. Anthropic disclosure: not required - the article never mentions Anthropic, Claude, or an Anthropic-operated product.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: DATE DISCREPANCY VERIFIED, NOT SILENTLY RESOLVED: the article claims the GitHub release page timestamps 2.32.0 to November 12, 2026 while the changelog dates it November 11, 2026. Checked both raw snapshots directly. source-0.html.gz (GitHub) shows the prominent 'released this <relative-time datetime="2026-11-12T11:20:48Z">12 Nov 11:20</relative-time>' banner -- November 12 is correct for 'the GitHub release page timestamp' as the article phrases it (there is also a GPG-signed-commit timestamp of 2026-11-11 15:17:36 UTC further down the page, which is a different, secondary datestamp, not the one the article cites). source-2.html.gz (raw CHANGELOG.md) shows '## 2.32.0 (2026-11-11)' -- November 11 exactly as claimed. So the one-day gap the writer flagged is real and both numbers are correctly attributed to their respective documents. The article does not attempt to explain or silently pick a 'true' date -- it states the gap in both the 'What We Know' section and again in 'What We Don't Know' ('Neither document explains the one-day gap...'), which is the correct claim-accuracy handling for an unexplained discrepancy between two primary sources. For 2.32.1, both GitHub (2026-11-19T19:23:10Z) and the changelog ('## 2.32.1 (2026-11-19)') agree on November 19 -- no discrepancy, and the article does not claim one. 2.31.0's October 20, 2026 AIC-preview date also matches the changelog ('## 2.31.0 (2026-10-20)') exactly. No other date, number, or quote in the article was found to be fabricated, misattributed, or unsupported by its cited source.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral throughout; no editorializing or sensationalism. Headline is a factual compound ('Fixes a Scheduler Bug...a Week After 2.32.0 Enabled...') rather than a paraphrased direct quote, so it is not held to exact-quote standards, and it accurately summarizes 'every job run by the scheduler fails' without overstating severity.
editor_notes.originality: No prior Machine Herald coverage of TimescaleDB exists (checked src/content/articles/ for any 'timescaledb' mention — only a QuestDB article from 2026-08 came up, which is unrelated). This is a genuinely new topic; not a duplicate of any recent or existing article.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Well-sourced, accurately hedged News piece on a real TimescaleDB patch release. The one-day date discrepancy the writer flagged between the GitHub release page and the CHANGELOG for 2.32.0 is real (verified against raw snapshots: GitHub shows November 12, 2026; changelog shows November 11, 2026) and the article handles it correctly by reporting both dates with attribution and flagging the gap as unexplained rather than silently resolving it. No fabricated or misattributed claims found after reading all 4 raw source snapshots. Featured candidacy: 0 - routine incremental bugfix-release coverage for a defined database-operator audience, not broad or exceptional.
